ai-outreach.text: Every day, up to 20 new prospect companies are picked up from HubSpot.
In n8n, each company with a website goes to Apollo.
Apollo fills in what the company does, its size and revenue, and HubSpot is updated.
Hunter.io lists the people there. The one who can act is picked: operations, IT or leadership, never an assistant or an intern.
Then the last month of news is searched for a real reason to write. Awards and press releases don't count. A $40M Series B does.
AI drafts the email in under 120 words, opening with that news. Invented results and stock lines are banned.
Nothing is sent until a person says yes in Slack. Here the reviewer rejects the draft, and says why.
The rewrite fixes only what was flagged: the subject. This time the reviewer approves, and it goes out through Gmail.
The prospect gets an email about their own news, sent to the person who can act on it.
Back in HubSpot, a company with no website, or none Apollo can find, is marked for a person, never guessed. So is a draft rejected twice.
Research, a real reason to write, and a person's yes before every send.

appointment-reminders.text: Patients get a text 24 hours before their visit, and another 2 hours before.
Every reminder comes from the clinic's own calendar.
On Tuesday at 8am, her 2-hour reminder is due. Anything already sent is skipped, then it waits briefly.
In that moment, a receptionist moves Ngozi to 3pm.
Seconds before sending, the live calendar is checked again, and the change is spotted.
The 10am reminder never goes out, and the reason is logged. Nothing is skipped silently.
A moved appointment counts as a new one. At 1pm, two hours before, she gets the right reminder: 3pm, not 10am.
Every reminder checked against the calendar, right before it sends.

client-lifecycle.text: A leed books a demo on the website, typing her phone number with a dash and a space.
Her name, email and phone are checked, and the number is cleaned into international format before any text goes out.
She's added to HubSpot, and a welcome text goes out through Termii. Whether it sent is read from Termii's reply, not assumed.
Less than 3 seconds after she pressed the button, the text is on her phone.
The sales team sees her in Slack, with the SMS confirmed and her HubSpot contact already made.
In HubSpot, she's a new contact with leed status New. Nobody typed a thing.
A form that arrives without a phone number goes to a Failed Leeds sheet, so nothing breaks and nothing is lost.
When she pays through Stripe, her HubSpot contact is looked up. If HubSpot is briefly down, it tries again, up to 3 times.
Her plan and last payment date are updated, and the payment is logged. A payer missing from HubSpot would email the team instead.
Every Monday at eight thirty in the morning, the payment log becomes a weekly report, sent by email and Slack.
The ops manager's 45-minute Monday job now arrives on its own.
Three workflows that feed each other: leeds, payments and the Monday report.

content-pipeline.text: The blog owner types one keyword into a Google Sheet. That's the whole brief.
Every hour, n8n takes the next keyword. AI writes the article and both social posts, and code checks the length, the links and the limits.
The article and its AI-made image are saved in WordPress as a draft. Nothing is live yet.
A person reads the preview and presses Publish in Slack.
It checks nobody published it by hand, puts it live, and Buffer sends the X and LinkedIn posts.
The article is live, with its own illustration and links to related posts on the blog.
On X it's short and direct. On LinkedIn it's longer and conversational.
Another keyword overlaps 83% with a post the blog already has. It's marked Duplicate, and nothing is written.
Every Monday, Search Console shows searches where the blog sits just off page one. The best become new keywords.
One keyword becomes a published, illustrated, shared article, with one approval in between.

crm-follow-ups.text: A new leed lands in HubSpot. That alone starts her sequence.
n8n receives her details: her area, her budget and what she asked about.
AI writes a first email around those details. If one is missing, it simply leaves it out.
It's sent from Gmail, the thread is saved, and HubSpot marks her In Sequence.
It lands in her inbox, reading like the agent wrote it.
No reply after three days? A follow-up goes out in the same thread, not as a new email.
On day seven she replies at eight fifty-eight, two minutes before the next follow-up was due.
A second workflow spots her reply and matches it to her thread.
Seconds before sending, her status is checked again. The follow-up is held back, so she's never chased after replying.
HubSpot moves her to Responded, and the agent gets a task to call her back.
A personal first email, timed follow-ups, and a clean handoff the moment she replies.

dental-chatbot.text: A visitor opens the website chat. The assistant answers naturally, then asks the next question.
It qualifies them in conversation, not with a form: new or existing, which service, and when.
Behind the chat, the AI reads the conversation. Then a switch picks the route: book, nurture or emergency.
The times it offers come from the live calendar, never from the AI.
It offers the real open times. The visitor picks 10am.
In that same moment, a staff member books 10am for someone else.
Right before booking, the slot is checked again. The clash is caught, so nobody is double-booked.
The visitor is offered the times still free, and 11am is booked.
It goes straight into the practice calendar, with the patient's details and what they came for.
Urgent symptoms skip booking entirely. The visitor gets a safety message straight away.
Emergencies and leeds not ready to book are logged, so the team can follow up.
Triage, live booking and follow-up, with no staff needed from the first hello.

multichannel-intake.text: A clinic sends a request through the website form, and gets a reference number on screen straight away.
Bots are quietly ignored, and broken forms are sent back to be fixed. This one is valid, so it gets its reference.
Emails and staff notes join the same path. The request is saved before the AI runs, so nothing is lost if the AI fails.
AI picks a category and urgency from approved options only, suggests the next step and drafts a reply. Code checks every answer.
Only Critical and High requests ping the team, with the next step and a link to the record.
Website, email and staff notes all land in one table. A reply to an earlier email is marked as a follow-up.
The same request sent twice? The second copy is caught at the duplicate check, even if the spacing changes.
Logged the moment it arrives, sorted by AI, and the team only hears about what can't wait.

office-assistant.text: One email, three asks: an invoice to pay, a revised deck by 2pm, and a meeting to move.
One AI step reads it, attachment included. The invoice decides the lane, and the deadline and the meeting become flags.
Code checks the answer first. A lane it doesn't know would stop the run, instead of filing the email in the wrong place.
Acme already has a folder, so the invoice is filed there. The email is starred, and a reminder is set.
The follow-up goes in the calendar at the next 9am or 2pm slot: 9am, well before the 2pm deadline.
The real emergency is starred. The coffee catch-up, the signed contract and the report go to General: a PDF isn't automatically an invoice.
An invoice that arrives as a photo is read by AI, so it still counts.
Luminary Print Co is a new vendor, so its folder is created on this first invoice, and the photo is filed inside.
Sorted, filed, starred and reminded, and it never sends anything in the agency's name.

opportunity-feed.text: Every morning at 10am, it reads the new posts on Remotive, a remote job board. Upwork or Indeed can be plugged in the same way.
In n8n, posts it has seen before are dropped. AI scores the rest, and must copy one line from each post as proof.
Code then searches the real post for that line. It's there, word for word, so this job is a fit: 10 out of 10.
Another post also scored as a fit, but the AI's line isn't in the post at all. No proof, no post: a person checks it instead.
Every post is logged in Airtable with its score and the quote behind it.
One message each morning: the fit with its proof, the post to check, and a pitch idea for a company still doing data entry by hand.
If Remotive is down or empty, the team is told today's jobs weren't checked, not a misleading "no jobs today".
An hour of scrolling becomes one short message, and every fit comes with its proof.

order-alerts.text: Chioma sees one of our ads and orders a sofa cover on the landing page.
Her order is placed. Every order is paid on delivery.
It arrives as an email in our Gmail inbox. Before, it could sit there unseen for up to two hours.
Every 15 minutes, Zapier checks the inbox for new emails that match the order search.
Only real orders match. Newsletters and other emails are ignored.
The order details go straight into a WhatsApp message.
Within 15 minutes of the order, my partner has it on WhatsApp, with everything needed to call her.
He calls Chioma to confirm while she’s still keen to buy.
From a new order to WhatsApp in 15 minutes, not two hours.

order-extraction.text: Over a thousand past orders sat in our Gmail inbox, one email each, with no customer list.
Each product had its own order form, so no two emails looked quite the same.
One run of the workflow pulls in every old order email, skips any already saved, and works through the rest.
For each email, AI reads it the way a person would, and pulls out the customer, product and price.
An order is only saved if it has a usable phone number. This one does.
Behind it, a second workflow reads and checks each order, and takes bundle quantities from the price table.
Order after order, the sheet fills up: all one thousand, one hundred and forty-five, in a single day.
An email with no usable phone number isn't guessed at. It goes to review, with the reason.
Failed checks and duplicates wait in the Invalid tab, so nothing is lost.
Now every past buyer is one search away, so a new launch can start with people who already bought.
From a buried inbox to a customer list we can sell to.

quote-requests.text: A hospital asks for a quote. The email lists no items: all 12 are spread across five attachments, one of them a photo.
Every two minutes, n8n checks the inbox, skips anything it has already handled, and finds the attachments.
Each file is read according to its type. PDFs, text and spreadsheets directly, and the photo by AI.
AI pulls out every item as the customer wrote it. The same product and quantity, listed in two attachments, is counted once.
Each item is matched to the catalog, model number first. The price always comes from the catalog, never from the AI.
Every line is saved in Airtable: the customer's words, the file it came from, the match and the price.
Nothing goes out unapproved. Staff see every match and the subtotal in Slack, and press Approve.
The quote lands in the customer's own thread. Delivery and VAT aren't in the catalog, so they're promised, not invented.
An item the supplier doesn't stock is marked to be confirmed, left out of the subtotal, and the request is flagged.
Every attachment read, every price from the catalog, and a person approves every reply.

solar-leads.text: A homeowner asks for a free solar assessment on the company's website.
In n8n, the form is checked and returning leeds are spotted. Then the address is looked up.
Geoapify matches it to a real building, 98% sure. Anything under 90% stops here, and nothing is researched.
The public property record confirms the owner on the deed, the roof and the size of the home.
N. R. E. L. gives the sunlight on that exact roof, month by month.
And the EIA gives the state's power price, saved for a month so Texas isn't looked up twice.
AI scores the leed from 0 to 100, with its reasons and concerns.
In HubSpot, the leed arrives scored and tiered, before anyone picks up the phone.
A hot leed gets a first email within minutes. It only uses facts the system is sure of, so no promised savings.
Another leed looks strong, but the deed shows a different owner, and the county says the roof is metal, not flat.
So it goes to a person on WhatsApp, whatever its score. So does an address that can't be verified.
Researched before anyone calls, checked against public records, and followed up in minutes.

voice-receptionist.text: Ada calls the clinic to book a cleaning.
The AI receptionist answers straight away, and asks what she needs.
The agent asks the workflow for open times. A switch sends it down the availability path.
A sheet points it to the Abuja branch’s own calendar, and it reads that day’s bookings.
It finds the free one-hour slots, never the lunch hour, and sends back the first three.
Ada picks 5pm, and the agent reads her name and number back to check them.
Meanwhile, someone at the clinic books 5pm for another patient.
Before booking, the workflow checks 5pm again. It has just been taken.
So it finds three new times and sends those back instead.
The agent tells Ada 5pm has gone and offers the new times.
4pm is still free, so the booking goes into the Abuja calendar.
The agent confirms on the call. A short while later, a text goes out through Termii.
The booking sits in the Abuja calendar, with her name, number and the reason for the visit.
Ada gets a text with the branch, date and time.
Every call answered, every booking in the right branch’s diary.

whatsapp-bakery.text: A customer orders the way they'd text a friend: three items, three different days, one message.
Plain rules answer greetings, menus and YES for free. This message is a real order, so it goes on to the AI.
The AI reads it against the real menu and the bakery's calendar, and finds three orders.
Then code checks every detail. Prices come from the menu, never from the AI.
One message becomes three orders, each with its own day and price.
Nothing is final until the customer replies YES. Then each order gets its own number.
All three land in the bakery's order book, clean and priced.
Voice notes work too. Ask for bread it doesn't sell, on a day it's closed, and it says so instead of guessing.
No number given? It asks, instead of guessing a quantity.
At 6pm every evening, orders nobody confirmed within 48 hours are marked Expired.
Then tomorrow's bake list is built from the confirmed orders and emailed.
Staff start the day with item totals and every pickup, with nothing retyped.
Messy messages in, clean and confirmed orders out.

whatsapp-receipts.text: Tunde, a driver, buys fuel and gets a paper receipt.
He opens the company’s WhatsApp chat and snaps a photo of it.
He sends the photo. That’s all he has to do.
The photo reaches the workflow in n8n, and it starts.
It checks the message is a photo or a PDF before going any further.
The receipt file is downloaded from WhatsApp.
Photos and PDFs are read differently. This one is a photo.
AI reads the vendor, date, total, tax and category, and flags anything it isn’t sure of.
The sender’s number is matched to the driver list in Airtable.
His name is attached. An unknown number would be saved as Unknown Driver, never dropped.
The reading and the driver are put together as one record.
Every field was read clearly, so it carries on. An unclear receipt would go to a review log instead.
It looks for this month’s folder in Google Drive.
The folder already exists, so no duplicate is made.
The receipt is pointed at the October 2026 folder.
The photo is uploaded, named by date, vendor and driver.
In Google Drive, it lands in October 2026, easy to find without opening it.
Next, a row is added to the expense sheet.
Driver, vendor, date, total, tax, category and a link to the file, all in one row.
Finally, the driver gets a WhatsApp reply.
Tunde sees exactly what was logged, about a minute after sending it.
From a photo on WhatsApp to a filed, logged expense.
